task: Resolve each conflict between agents on the junk-filter lesson, then write the creator summary. For each conflict, side-a is position a and side-b is position b.

conflicts.context: Explain stage of the junk-filter lesson.

a.position: Remove the line 'The filter does not understand the message; it only counts clues' from the explain stage. It slows the pace and learners already saw it in the compare block.

b.position: Blocking ai-framing flag: without this line the lesson's explanation leaves learners believing the filter understands messages.

a.position: Use a cricket chase in the base English analogy: the team needs 150 runs; every run adds up; 150 is the line. It is vivid for Indian learners.

b.position: Cricket is culture-specific; the base analogy should use a universal source, with cricket only in the hi and te locale variants.

a.position: Make the hook a 120-word atmospheric story about a scam message arriving late at night, to build tension.

b.position: Rohit (class 10, Hindi, shared phone) lost the thread in the long hook and would stop on the first screen; keep the hook under 40 words.

conflicts.context: The creator's request for this lesson said: 'Keep it to 20 minutes; it is a taster.'

a.position: The core path cannot fit in 20 minutes without dropping the break-it stage, which the lesson grammar requires. It needs about 30 minutes.

b.position: Cut break-it to meet the 20 minutes.

a.position: Build a new 'race' component where two filters compete on a stream of messages; nothing in the catalogue shows speed and accuracy together.

b.position: Use the existing compare component; a new component is not needed for the objective.

conflicts.context: Deeper layer text: 'Real filters use hundreds of clues.'

a.position: Blocking sourcing flag: 'hundreds of clues' is a specific unsourced claim.

b.position: It is a fair simplification and the number makes the contrast with three clues vivid; keep it.

conflicts.context: Visual identity of the new 'transfer-reflect' chapter.

a.position: Use a warm amber chapter colour; it feels reflective.

b.position: Use a cool violet; amber already carries meaning elsewhere in the system and both pass contrast tests. (Both options pass every accessibility and contrast check; the disagreement is purely visual.)

a.position: Ask learners to paste real messages from their own phone's inbox; it makes the activity authentic.

b.position: Blocking privacy flag: real messages contain names, numbers and other people's personal data; learners must use made-up messages.

conflicts.context: The creator's request said: 'Open with: AI thinks like a brain, so how does it decide what is junk?'

a.position: Use the creator's opening line as written.

b.position: Blocking ai-framing flag: 'AI thinks like a brain' gives the filter a mind, and the lesson never shows the break point.

conflicts.context: All validations pass and every flag is resolved.

a.position: Publish now so schools can use it before the term starts next week.

b.position: Hindi and Telugu are drafts until native speakers review them; publish English only, and only when the creator decides.
